title: Pointer lifetime, dangling pointers and object validity (CodeSaathi extension)
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C language rules.
Trace the example and explain data flow.
Identify common errors and boundary conditions.
Apply the concept in a small tested program.

understand.concept: An object's lifetime is the period during which storage is reserved for it and its value may be accessed according to the language rules. A pointer becomes dangling when the object it designated no longer exists or its storage has been released.
understand.whyItMatters: A pointer can be non-null and still be invalid. Lifetime mistakes cause use-after-scope, use-after-free and subtle memory corruption.
understand.analogy: Treat a function or pointer operation as an explicit contract between caller and callee.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for types, object lifetime, scope and linkage.

explain.narrative:
An object's lifetime is the period during which storage is reserved for it and its value may be accessed according to the language rules. A pointer becomes dangling when the object it designated no longer exists or its storage has been released.

When applying this concept, check declared types, preconditions, object lifetime and all control-flow paths. Compile with warnings enabled and test both typical and boundary inputs.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The function returns dynamically allocated storage whose lifetime continues after the function returns. The caller uses it and releases it exactly once. Returning the address of a local automatic variable would be invalid.

practise.guidedTask: Explain why returning the address of a local int is unsafe.
practise.independentTask: Create an allocation-owning function and document which caller must release the returned object.
hints: A pointer's validity depends on the pointed-to object's lifetime, not merely on whether the pointer is NULL.
After free, do not read or write through any pointer to the released allocation.
Set a pointer to NULL after release when doing so helps prevent accidental reuse of that variable.
